commenti.body: Yeah, I think the title is a play on both Steven Yeun's "hobby" and the protagonist's resentment at both his wealth and at taking the girl from him. I think the movie is not very kind to the protagonist and paints him as possessive of her, rather than actually concerned for her wellbeing.

The movie definitely enjoys playing in uncertainty, and I think that’s where it’s strongest. 

The burning seems to apply to all of the emotions tied to that uncertainty. His curiosity about which greenhouse is going to burn; the uncertainty about their relationship dynamic; his jealousy and confusion about the new dynamic when she returns; and finally the way she seems to have vanished, without his knowing if she’s cutting him off or if she may have been murdered. All of those get under his skin and burn him up more and more as time goes on.

I can't quite remember what he said exactly but I saw in an interview the director mentioned something about this being this genesis of the film. Sort of this low level anxiety we all feel that something is uncertain or "off" and he was trying to convey that feeling through the film.

This is one of the first movies I think really nailed the feeling of subtle anxiety. All these little clues and details add up to support the hunch that the worst thing imaginable has happened, but it’s somehow both ambiguous and plain as day at the same time. So if you want to believe everything is ok you’d be deluding yourself, and though you might want to, you just cant go against your intuition. Awesome film

My reading of the film is a bit different. I interpreted it as the poor going through the world in a daze, barely comprehending the world around them. The rich on the other hand rightfully see them as lesser beings which they use for entertainment and discard them without a second thought once they are bored of them. 

A popular theory seems to be that Ben did not kill his "victims" but rather he may have helped them start life anew, give them new identities and money to run away with. But I think it seemed pretty clear from the yawning and his friends making fun of the girls he brought that he thought they were beneath him or beyond saving. He calls the greenhouses he burns "useless, filthy, unpleasant-looking". It seemed like he was targeting poor adventurous women specifically, which is why I think that if he didn't kill them, at the very least he toyed with them for his own amusement. He wasn't saving them.

The ending is an impotent power fantasy of the revenge that poor people wish they could have on the rich once they get a brief moment of clarity as to the reality of their situation.

One of the best movies ever imo. Few have captured the listlessness and uncertainty felt within modern life like Burning has. I don’t care to try and solve the plot like a puzzle and I think it’s a waste of time. It defies the need to pontificate. I often ponder the images, sounds, and feelings of want, confusion, and day-dreaming exhibited in the movie. Masterpiece, and that’s a far-overused term.

I recommend reading the Haruki Murakami short story this film is adapted from as well as the Faulkner short story "Barn Burning". I love this movie but it's been a few years since I've seen it so I can't remember my thoughts on the meaning, but the short stories should give some insight. The Murakami story was in The New Yorker so you can read it for free as long as you haven't already read all your free articles for the month.

Absolutely love this movie. Director Lee Chang Dong talks about the meaning if the film in an interview - you can find it on YouTube. 
There is intentional ambiguity as to whether Ben  killed Haemi or it was all imagined and written by the protagonist. 
Lee talks about how young people today are subject to so much uncertainty, and feel so helplessness against the powers that be. And this is a big part of the film's meaning.

I see Ben as the embodiment of capitalism and the way it carelessly wastes the things we value in this world. To burn a greenhouse is to burn mother nature and the plants that give us life. But we know this is a metaphor for Haemi and that Ben is actually killing girls. But I think the metaphor works again in reverse and that Haemi is a representation of nature herself. By killing poor unknown women like this Ben is carelessly discarding not only women/precious human beings, but also the poor as well as the innocence of nature. I think the scene where Haemi dances nude is meant to show that she represents the freedom and naked innocence of nature.

Jongsu is jealous of Ben because he wants Haemi, but he also cares about her and wants to protect her. He sees this smug, rich guy for whom life is a game and is no problem and feels a burning anger at him. But he also feels the burning “big hunger” for something better than this world where the poor and innocent are discarded, where the rich have it incredibly easy and can use and destroy everything and everyone else, and there are no answers or actions you can take.

This movie resonated with me because I feel the big hunger and I resent the way our system discards and destroys the things I care about and I resent the guys like Ben in my life who don’t seem to care about anything besides enjoying the easiest lifestyles on earth at the expense of others (he doesn’t even have a job. “I play” I think he says. Such a chilling and poignant line by Lee Chang-dong). I think the movie accurately shows that yeah, Jongsu might be a bit jealous on some level, but the real difference is that he actually has a sense of humanity and right vs wrong whereas Ben does not.
